1.note: The expression **year of two** uses a cardinal number where your language might use an ordinal number, since it refers to the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **two**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the second year]

Daniel is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [Nebuchadnezzar dreamed]

The expression **his spirit was troubled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And this troubled his spirit]

Daniel is using **his sleep finished for him** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Nebuchadnezzar was unable to sleep. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he could not sleep]

2.note: The terms **magicians**, **enchanters**, and **sorcerers** are different kinds of people who were thought to have special knowledge or powers, such as interpreting dreams, using magic, or communicating with spirits. If your readers would not be familiar with what these are, you could use the names of similar people that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [the users of magic and the spell-casters and the fortune-tellers]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in the presence of the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of the king]

3.note: Nebuchadnezzar is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [I dreamed]

The expression **is troubled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it troubles my spirit]

4.note: The Chaldeans are using **live forever** as a common expression of the culture to mean “may you live for a long time.” It was a respectful way to greet a king. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you live for a long time]

The Chaldeans are speaking of themselves in the third person as **your servants** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to us, your humble servants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and we will interpret it for you]

5.note: The expression **and was saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly, here and in its many other occurrences in this book.

The king is using **The word from me is firm** as a common expression of the culture to mean “my decision is final.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My decision is final]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and interpret it for me]

The expression **you will be made** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will have your limbs cut off]

The expression **your houses will be made a rubbish heap** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will turn your houses into a rubbish heap]

6.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and interpret it for me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of honor, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will honor you very much]

7.note: Even though the Chaldeans are addressing the king directly, they are speaking of him in the third person as **the king** and of themselves in the third person as **his servants** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form using the second person and the first person. Alternate translation: [O king, please tell us your servants the dream]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and we will interpret it for you]

8.note: See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the king is using it to indicate that what follows is the reason for what precedes. Alternate translation: [because]

The king is using **you are buying time** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you are trying to gain more time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are trying extend the time allotted]

9.note: The king is using **your decree is one** as a common expression of the culture to mean “there is only one verdict for you all.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is only one verdict for you all]

The expression **the time is changed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [circumstances change]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you interpret it correctly]

10.note: The Chaldeans are not referring to a specific **man**. They mean people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]

See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the wise men are using it to indicate that what follows shows why what precedes is true. Alternate translation: [you may be sure of this because] or [after all,]

11.note: The Chaldeans are using **flesh** to represent human beings, who are mortal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

12.note: See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the author is using it to indicate that follows is the result of what he has just described. Alternate translation: [Because of this] or [As a result]

The terms **became angry** and **became very furious** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [became extremely angry]

13.note: The expression **the wise men were to be killed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that people should kill the wise men]

The expression **to be killed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And they sought Daniel and his friends in order to kill them]

14.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **prudence** and **discretion**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [prudently and discreetly]
The word **Arioch** is the name of a man.

16.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he might explain to the king what the dream meant]

18.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mercies**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that they might seek to be treated mercifully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mystery**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what was hidden] or [what they did not know]

19.note: The expression **the mystery was revealed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God revealed the mystery to Daniel]

20.note: David is saying what he wants to happen. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech, and follow the decision you have made as a team about how speakers will express in such contexts what they want to happen. Alternate translation: [I desire for God’s name to be blessed]

The expression **be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May people bless the name of God]
Daniel is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. Alternate translation: [May God be blessed]

“His name, of God” is a doubling of reference. The phrase names God twice, once by pronoun, “name,” and once explicitly as “God.” It might seem that the expression **his name, of God** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [May God be blessed]
Here, **his name** represents God himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [God himself]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom** and **power**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [being wise and being mighty]

Daniel is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **from eternity** and **to eternity**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for all time]

21.q: יָהֵ֤ב חָכְמְתָ⁠א֙ לְ⁠חַכִּימִ֔ין וּ⁠מַנְדְּעָ֖⁠א לְ⁠יָדְעֵ֥י בִינָֽה
21.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [the one giving wisdom and understanding to those who are wise]

Daniel is using the adjective **wise** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to wise people] or [to those who are wise]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **knowledge** and **understanding**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and enabling those who can discern to know things]

21.q: יָהֵ֤ב חָכְמְתָ⁠א֙ לְ⁠חַכִּימִ֔ין וּ⁠מַנְדְּעָ֖⁠א לְ⁠יָדְעֵ֥י בִינָֽה
21.note: This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

22.note: Daniel is using the plural adjectives **the deep** and **the hidden** as nouns to mean certain kinds of things. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [deep things and hidden things]

The terms **the deep** and **the hidden** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [things that are very difficult to know] or [things that are very obscure]

22.q: יָדַע֙ מָ֣ה בַ⁠חֲשׁוֹכָ֔⁠א ו⁠נהיר⁠א עִמֵּ֥⁠הּ שְׁרֵֽא
22.note: Daniel is speaking of hidden things as if they were **darkness** and of what God knows as if it were **light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he knows what is secret, and understanding resides with him]

23.note: Daniel is speaking of his ancestors as if they were his **fathers**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God of my ancestors]
By **we**, Daniel means himself and his friends but not the one to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

24.note: See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the author is using it to indicate that follows is the result of what he has just described. Alternate translation: [Consequently]

25.note: The word **that** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Arioch is using **the sons of the captivity of Judah** as a common expression of the culture to mean the people who had been taken away from Judah into exile. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the exiles from Judah who]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those captured from Judah who]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the dream means]

26.note: The word **Belteshazzar** is the Babylonian name given to Daniel.

28.note: Daniel is using **at the end of days** as a common expression of the culture to mean a future time. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in days to come]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a connecting word or phrase to show that **Your dream and the visions of your head** explains what Daniel means when he says that God has made the king know what will happen in the future. Alternate translation: [Your dream, that is, the visions of your head]

Daniel is using **the visions of your head** as a common expression of the culture to mean the things that Nebuchadnezzar saw in his mind while he was dreaming. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the images you saw in your mind]

29.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thoughts**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you were thinking]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mysteries**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [hidden things]

30.note: The expression **this mystery has been revealed to me** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God has revealed this mystery to me]

Daniel is using the adjective **living** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [more than anyone else who is alive] or [more than any other human being]

The pronoun **they** does not refer to any specific people here. Daniel uses it in an indefinite way to mean that the interpretation would be made known to the king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the king may come to know]

Daniel is speaking of the mind as if it were the **heart**, because the people of this culture associated thinking with the heart. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the thoughts of your mind]

31.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **appearance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and it looked terrifying]

Daniel is using the term **behold** to focus King Nebuchadnezzar’s attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look]

The expression **was great and its splendor was exceeding** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [This statue was very large, and it gleamed with extraordinary splendor]

The expression **its appearance was terrifying** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it terrified those who saw it]

32.q: חֲד֥וֹ⁠הִי וּ⁠דְרָע֖וֹ⁠הִי דִּ֣י כְסַ֑ף מְע֥וֹ⁠הִי וְ⁠יַרְכָתֵ֖⁠הּ דִּ֥י נְחָֽשׁ
32.note: Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [its chest and arms were of silver; its belly and its thighs were of bronze]

33.q: שָׁק֖וֹ⁠הִי דִּ֣י פַרְזֶ֑ל רַגְל֕וֹ⁠הִי מנ⁠הון דִּ֣י פַרְזֶ֔ל ו⁠מנ⁠הון דִּ֥י חֲסַֽף
33.note: Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that its legs {were} of iron. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [its legs were of iron; some of its feet were of iron and some of them were of clay]

34.note: The expression **a stone was cut out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone cut out a stone]

Here, **hands** represents the effort or action of human beings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but not by human effort]

35.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **chaff** is light and easily blown away by the wind, so the crushed pieces of the statue were completely scattered and disappeared. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as light and scattered as the chaff of the threshing floors of summer]

The expression **any place was not found for them** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one could find any trace of them]

Daniel is speaking of the kingdom that God will establish as if it were **a great mountain** that **filled all of the earth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [grew into a kingdom that spread throughout the whole earth]

36.note: By **we**, Daniel means himself but not the king to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And we will tell the king what it means]

37.note: Daniel is using **the king of kings** as a common expression of the culture to mean a supreme king who rules over other kings. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are the greatest king, ruling over all other kings]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **the power**, **the strength**, and **the glory**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the ability to rule powerfully, to rule strongly, and to be honored greatly]

38.note: Daniel is using **the sons of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean human beings in general. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

Daniel is not referring to a specific **beast** or **bird**. He means beasts and birds in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the wild animals, and the birds of the sky]
Here, **your hand** represents your power and control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into your power]

Daniel is speaking of Nebuchadnezzar as if he were the head of gold on the statue. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are like the head of gold]

39.note: Here, **earthward from you** represents being inferior. since the earth is generally below people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [inferior to you]

40.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **iron** is strong and crushes other things, so **a fourth kingdom** will be strong and will crush the kingdoms before it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [strong just as iron is strong]

See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, Daniel is using it to indicate that the first part of this sentence is equivalent to the second part. Alternate translation: [just as]

41.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **firmness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how firm iron is]

The expression **For some of the firmness of iron will be in it** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [This kingdom will have some of the strength of iron in it]
See how you translated this expression in the similar context in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [just as]

42.q: וְ⁠אֶצְבְּעָת֙ רַגְלַיָּ֔⁠א מנ⁠הון פַּרְזֶ֖ל ו⁠מנ⁠הון חֲסַ֑ף מִן־קְצָ֤ת מַלְכוּתָ⁠א֙ תֶּהֱוֵ֣ה תַקִּיפָ֔ה וּ⁠מִנַּ֖⁠הּ תֶּהֱוֵ֥ה תְבִירָֽה
42.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the toes of the feet** were **some iron and some clay**, so is the kingdom composed of both strong and brittle elements. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as the toes of the feet were partly iron and partly clay, so will some of the kingdom be strong and some of it will be brittle]
In each part of the verse, you could put the **clay** before the **iron** in order to put the new information before the old information. The UST models one way to do that.

43.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the people of the divided kingdom, that is, its rulers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the rulers of the divided kingdom will be mixing themselves]

Daniel is speaking of human descendants as if they were **seed** that a man plants. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [through their offspring]

The point of this comparison is that just as **iron** does not mix itself with **clay**, so the rulers of this kingdom will not remain united with one another. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as iron does not stay mixed with clay, so those rulers will not remain united]

44.note: The expression **a kingdom that will not be destroyed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a kingdom that no one will ever destroy]

The expression **the kingdom will not be left to another people** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no other people will take over the kingdom]

Daniel is stating the pronoun **it** separately, even though the verb translated as **it will stand** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that this kingdom, unlike the kingdoms that came before it, will endure forever. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [but God’s kingdom will stand forever]

45.note: Daniel is speaking of the kingdom that God will establish as if it were a stone that was cut from a mountain, but not by hands. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God set up a kingdom, pictured as a stone cut from a mountain but not by human hands]

The expression **a stone was cut from a mountain** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone cut a stone from a mountain]

The expression **confirmed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God has confirmed what it means]

46.note: Falling on his face was a symbolic action by which Nebuchadnezzar showed great honor and reverence toward Daniel. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [bowed down to the ground to show honor]

47.note: The king is using **the God of gods and the Lord of kings** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Daniel’s God is supreme over all other gods and over all kings. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [supreme over all other gods and over all kings]

48.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he made him chief of the governors]

49.note: Here, **the gate of the king** represents the king’s court, where officials carried out the business of the government. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [But Daniel remained at the royal court]
